4→ 5→

Privacy-first encrypted cloud storage with decentralized persistence

6→ 7→--- 8→ 9→## What is CipherBox 10→ 11→CipherBox is a **technology demonstrator** for privacy-first cloud storage. All encryption happens client-side — the server never sees plaintext data, file names, or encryption keys. Files are stored on IPFS for decentralized persistence, keys are derived deterministically via Web3Auth so the same user always gets the same vault regardless of login method, and data can be exported for independent recovery without CipherBox. 12→ 13→## Acknowledgements 14→ 15→This project is inspired by discussions and planning while working on [ChainSafe Files](https://github.com/chainsafe/ui-monorepo). A massive shout-out to all the colleagues I got to work with on the original ChainSafe Files project, who unknowingly contributed to this phoenix rising out of the ashes. 16→ 17→## Features 18→ 19→- **Authentication** — Web3Auth MPC Core Kit: email OTP, Google OAuth, magic link, external wallet. MFA via device factor. Same user + any auth method = same vault. 20→- **Encryption** — Client-side AES-256-GCM for files and metadata. ECIES secp256k1 key wrapping (per-file, per-folder random keys). Streaming AES-CTR for large files. 21→- **File Management** — Upload, download, rename, move, delete. Nested folders up to 20 levels. Drag-and-drop. 22→- **Sharing** — User-to-user sharing with ECIES re-wrapping. Link sharing with time-limited access tokens. 23→- **Search** — Client-side encrypted search index across file and folder names. 24→- **Versioning** — File history with point-in-time restore. 25→- **Sync** — Multi-device via IPNS polling (~30s). Conflict detection and resolution. 26→- **Desktop** — macOS, Windows, and Linux via Tauri v2. Virtual filesystem mount (FUSE-T / WinFSP / libfuse). Background sync with system tray. 27→- **Recycle Bin** — 30-day soft-delete with restore. 28→- **TEE Republishing** — Automatic IPNS record refresh every 3 hours via Phala Cloud. Zero-knowledge: keys decrypted only inside hardware enclaves. 29→- **Data Portability** — Full vault export (JSON + encrypted blobs). Standalone recovery with private key — no CipherBox required. 30→ 31→## Architecture Overview 32→ 33→```text 34→┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ 35→│ Web / Desktop│────▶│ CipherBox │────▶│ PostgreSQL │ 36→│ (Client) │ │ API │ │ (Metadata) │ 37→└──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └───────────────┘ 38→ │ │ 39→ │ Encrypted │ Relay 40→ │ blobs │ 41→ ▼ ▼ 42→┌──────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ 43→│ IPFS │ │ TEE Worker │ 44→│ (Storage) │ │ (IPNS Refresh)│ 45→└──────────────┘ └───────────────┘ 46→``` 47→ 48→The client encrypts everything locally. The API is a zero-knowledge relay — it stores encrypted keys and routes IPFS/IPNS operations but never accesses plaintext. For full cryptographic details, see [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md). 49→ 50→## Tech Stack 51→ 52→| Component | Technology | 53→| :----------------- | :-------------------------------------------- | 54→| **Frontend** | React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS | 55→| **Backend** | Node.js + NestJS + TypeScript | 56→| **Database** | PostgreSQL 16 | 57→| **Job Queue** | BullMQ + Redis | 58→| **Key Derivation** | Web3Auth MPC Core Kit | 59→| **Storage** | IPFS via Kubo / Pinata | 60→| **Desktop** | Tauri v2 + FUSE-T / WinFSP | 61→| **TEE** | Phala Cloud (IPNS republishing) | 62→| **Crypto** | Web Crypto API (AES-256-GCM, ECIES secp256k1) | 63→ 64→## Project Structure 65→ 66→```text 67→cipher-box/ 68→├── apps/ 69→│ ├── api/ # NestJS backend 70→│ ├── web/ # React frontend 71→│ └── desktop/ # Tauri v2 desktop app 72→├── packages/ 73→│ ├── crypto/ # Shared encryption library 74→│ └── api-client/ # Generated typed API client 75→├── tee-worker/ # Phala Cloud TEE worker 76→├── tests/ 77→│ ├── e2e/ # Playwright E2E tests 78→│ └── e2e-desktop/ # Desktop E2E tests 79→└── docker/ # Docker Compose (PostgreSQL, IPFS, Redis) 80→``` 81→ 82→## Getting Started 83→ 84→```bash 85→docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d 86→pnpm install 87→pnpm dev # starts API (:3000) + web (:5173) 88→``` 89→ 90→See [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) for full setup instructions including desktop app, testing, and environment configuration. 91→ 92→## Documentation 93→ 94→| Document | Description | 95→| :------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- | 96→| [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) | Encryption hierarchy, key derivation, threat model | 97→| [docs/DEVELOPMENT.md](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) | Local setup, running, testing | 98→| [docs/AUTHENTICATION_ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/AUTHENTICATION_ARCHITECTURE.md) | Auth flow details | 99→| [docs/METADATA_SCHEMAS.md](docs/METADATA_SCHEMAS.md) | All metadata object schemas | 100→| [docs/VAULT_EXPORT_FORMAT.md](docs/VAULT_EXPORT_FORMAT.md) | Export/recovery data format | 101→| [docs/DATABASE_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md](docs/DATABASE_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL.md) | Migration discipline | 102→| [00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/](00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/) | Frozen v1 specifications (PRD, API, Data Flows, Client Spec) | 103→ 104→## License 105→ 106→[MIT](LICENSE) 107→

1→# Architecture
     2→
     3→CipherBox implements layered, zero-knowledge encryption where **all user data is encrypted client-side before leaving the device**. The server and storage layer never see plaintext — not file contents, not file names, not folder names, not timestamps, not file sizes.
     4→
     5→## System Overview
     6→
     7→```text
     8→User Device (Web/Desktop)
     9→        ↓ Auth (4 methods)
    10→CipherBox Backend (JWT)
    11→        ↓
    12→Web3Auth Network (Key Derivation)
    13→        ↓ ECDSA Private Key (RAM only!)
    14→User Device ← Vault Data ← PostgreSQL
    15→        ↓ Encrypted Keys
    16→IPFS (Pinata) ← Encrypted Files
    17→        ↑
    18→TEE (Phala/Nitro) ← IPNS Republish (every 3h)
    19→```
    20→
    21→**Key Properties:**
    22→
    23→- Same user + any auth method → same keypair → same vault
    24→- TEE republishes IPNS records even when all devices are offline
    25→
    26→## Key Derivation
    27→
    28→Two paths produce the same `VaultKey` (a secp256k1 keypair):
    29→
    30→```text
    31→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    32→│                       KEY DERIVATION                                │
    33→├─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┤
    34→│  Web3Auth (Social Login)│  External Wallet (MetaMask, etc.)        │
    35→│                         │                                           │
    36→│  Google/Email/etc.      │  1. Sign deterministic EIP-712 message   │
    37→│        ↓                │  2. Normalize signature (low-S, EIP-2)   │
    38→│  Web3Auth Network       │  3. HKDF-SHA256:                         │
    39→│        ↓                │     salt  = "CipherBox-ECIES-v1"         │
    40→│  secp256k1 keypair      │     info  = wallet address (lowercase)   │
    41→│  (deterministic)        │     input = normalized signature          │
    42→│                         │        ↓                                  │
    43→│                         │  secp256k1 keypair (deterministic)       │
    44→├─────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┤
    45→│                              ↓                                      │
    46→│                   VaultKey (secp256k1)                               │
    47→│          ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐                    │
    48→│          │ Private Key: 32 bytes (RAM only!)   │                    │
    49→│          │ Public Key:  65 bytes (uncompressed) │                   │
    50→│          └─────────────────────────────────────┘                    │
    51→└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    52→```
    53→
    54→## Encryption Hierarchy
    55→
    56→Every key below the VaultKey is **randomly generated** (not derived) and **ECIES-wrapped** with the user's public key. Compromising one file key reveals nothing about other file keys.
    57→
    58→```text
    59→    VaultKey (secp256k1 keypair)
    60→    │
    61→    │  ECIES-unwrap
    62→    ├──────────────────────────────────────────┐
    63→    │                                          │
    64→    ▼                                          ▼
    65→ rootFolderKey (random 32B)          rootIpnsPrivateKey (Ed25519)
    66→    │                                          │
    67→    │  AES-256-GCM decrypt                     │  Signs IPNS records
    68→    ▼                                          ▼
    69→ Root Folder Metadata (encrypted JSON)     IPNS publish/resolve
    70→    │
    71→    │  Contains per-child entries:
    72→    │
    73→    ├── File Entries ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
    74→    │     name (encrypted)        ◄── only visible after       │
    75→    │     size (encrypted)            decrypting metadata       │
    76→    │     timestamps (encrypted)                                │
    77→    │     fileKeyEncrypted ──── ECIES-unwrap ──► fileKey (32B) │
    78→    │     fileIv (12B)                              │           │
    79→    │     cid (IPFS ref)            AES-256-GCM decrypt        │
    80→    │                                               ▼          │
    81→    │                                        File Contents     │
    82→    │                                                          │
    83→    ├── Subfolder Entries ─────────────────────────────────────┤
    84→    │     name (encrypted)        ◄── only visible after       │
    85→    │     timestamps (encrypted)      decrypting metadata      │
    86→    │     folderKeyEncrypted ── ECIES-unwrap ──► folderKey     │
    87→    │     ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted ─ ECIES-unwrap ► ipnsKey     │
    88→    │     ipnsName (k51...)                                    │
    89→    │          │                                               │
    90→    │          ▼                                               │
    91→    │     Subfolder Metadata (same structure, recursive)       │
    92→    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    93→```
    94→
    95→## Visibility Model
    96→
    97→```text
    98→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    99→│                    FULLY ENCRYPTED                               │
   100→│   (requires user's private key + folder key to access)          │
   101→│                                                                  │
   102→│   ✓ File contents              ✓ File names                     │
   103→│   ✓ Folder names               ✓ Folder structure / child list  │
   104→│   ✓ File sizes                 ✓ Creation timestamps            │
   105→│   ✓ Modification timestamps    ✓ All encryption keys            │
   106→│   ✓ IPNS private keys          ✓ File-to-folder relationships   │
   107→├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   108→│                    VISIBLE (Plaintext)                           │
   109→│   (required for IPFS/IPNS protocol operation)                   │
   110→│                                                                  │
   111→│   • IPFS CIDs (content-addressed hashes, no semantic meaning)  │
   112→│   • IPNS names (k51... public identifiers for folders)         │
   113→│   • Encrypted blob sizes (approximate original sizes)          │
   114→│   • Encryption IVs (required for decryption, not secret)       │
   115→│   • User's secp256k1 public key                                │
   116→├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   117→│                    NEVER STORED (RAM Only)                       │
   118→│                                                                  │
   119→│   • User's private key          • Decrypted file names          │
   120→│   • Decrypted folder metadata   • Decrypted file contents       │
   121→│   • Plaintext file/folder keys  • Wallet signatures             │
   122→└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   123→```
   124→
   125→## Cryptographic Primitives
   126→
   127→| Purpose                    | Algorithm                  | Parameters                               |
   128→| :------------------------- | :------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- |
   129→| File & metadata encryption | AES-256-GCM                | 256-bit key, 96-bit IV, 128-bit auth tag |
   130→| Key wrapping               | ECIES (secp256k1)          | Ephemeral keypair + AES-GCM              |
   131→| Key derivation (wallets)   | HKDF-SHA256                | 32-byte output, static salt              |
   132→| IPNS record signing        | Ed25519                    | 32-byte seed, 64-byte signatures         |
   133→| Random generation          | `crypto.getRandomValues()` | CSPRNG (Web Crypto API)                  |
   134→
   135→## Data Flows
   136→
   137→### File Upload
   138→
   139→```text
   140→  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   141→  │                    FILE UPLOAD FLOW                           │
   142→  │                                                              │
   143→  │  1. User selects "document.pdf"                              │
   144→  │         │                                                    │
   145→  │         ▼                                                    │
   146→  │  2. Generate random fileKey (32 bytes)                       │
   147→  │     Generate random IV (12 bytes)                            │
   148→  │         │                                                    │
   149→  │         ▼                                                    │
   150→  │  3. AES-256-GCM encrypt(plaintext, fileKey, IV)              │
   151→  │     → ciphertext ‖ auth_tag (16 bytes)                       │
   152→  │         │                                                    │
   153→  │         ▼                                                    │
   154→  │  4. ECIES wrap(fileKey, userPublicKey)                        │
   155→  │     → ephemeral_pubkey ‖ wrapped_key ‖ tag                   │
   156→  │         │                                                    │
   157→  │         ▼                                                    │
   158→  │  5. Clear plaintext fileKey from memory                      │
   159→  │         │                                                    │
   160→  │         ▼                                                    │
   161→  │  6. Upload encrypted blob → Pinata → IPFS → returns CID     │
   162→  │         │                                                    │
   163→  │         ▼                                                    │
   164→  │  7. Add to folder metadata:                                  │
   165→  │       { name, cid, fileKeyEncrypted, fileIv, size, ... }     │
   166→  │         │                                                    │
   167→  │         ▼                                                    │
   168→  │  8. Re-encrypt folder metadata with folderKey (AES-256-GCM)  │
   169→  │         │                                                    │
   170→  │         ▼                                                    │
   171→  │  9. Upload encrypted metadata → IPFS → new CID              │
   172→  │         │                                                    │
   173→  │         ▼                                                    │
   174→  │ 10. Publish IPNS record: /ipns/k51... → /ipfs/<new CID>     │
   175→  │     (signed with folder's Ed25519 private key)               │
   176→  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   177→```
   178→
   179→## Defense in Depth
   180→
   181→Each file key is protected by multiple nested layers. An attacker must break through all layers to access any file content:
   182→
   183→```text
   184→   File Content
   185→     └─ encrypted with ──► fileKey (random, unique per file)
   186→         └─ ECIES-wrapped with ──► User's Public Key
   187→             └─ stored inside ──► Folder Metadata
   188→                 └─ encrypted with ──► folderKey (random, unique per folder)
   189→                     └─ ECIES-wrapped with ──► User's Public Key
   190→                         └─ stored on ──► Server (zero-knowledge)
   191→```
   192→
   193→## Threat Model
   194→
   195→With full access to IPFS and the CipherBox server but without the user's private key:
   196→
   197→```text
   198→  IPFS (public network):
   199→
   200→    /ipfs/bafybei3a7x...   ← encrypted blob (file? folder? unknown)
   201→    /ipfs/bafybei9f2k...   ← encrypted blob (file? folder? unknown)
   202→    /ipfs/bafybeiqw8m...   ← encrypted blob (file? folder? unknown)
   203→
   204→  Without the user's private key:
   205→    ✗ Cannot read file contents
   206→    ✗ Cannot read file or folder names
   207→    ✗ Cannot determine folder structure
   208→    ✗ Cannot read timestamps or file sizes
   209→    ✗ Cannot determine which blobs are files vs. folders
   210→    ✓ Can see encrypted blob sizes (approximates original size)
   211→    ✓ Can see IPNS update frequency (usage pattern)
   212→```
   213→
   214→## Key Design Decisions
   215→
   216→### 1. Web3Auth for Key Derivation
   217→
   218→```text
   219→Email/Password/OAuth/Magic Link/External Wallet → Web3Auth → Same ECDSA keypair
   220→```
   221→
   222→### 2. Layered Encryption
   223→
   224→```text
   225→File (AES-256-GCM) → Metadata (AES-256-GCM) → Keys (ECIES)
   226→```
   227→
   228→### 3. Per-Folder IPNS
   229→
   230→```text
   231→Root IPNS → Folder1 IPNS → Folder2 IPNS (modular sharing-ready)
   232→```
   233→
   234→### 4. IPNS Polling Sync
   235→
   236→```text
   237→30s polling, no push infrastructure (MVP simple)
   238→```
   239→
   240→### 5. Zero-Knowledge Keys
   241→
   242→```text
   243→Server holds: Encrypted root key only
   244→Client holds: Private key (RAM only)
   245→```
   246→
   247→### 6. TEE-Based IPNS Republishing
   248→
   249→```text
   250→IPNS records expire after ~24h → TEE republishes every 3h
   251→Client encrypts ipnsPrivateKey with TEE public key (ECIES)
   252→TEE decrypts in hardware, signs, zeroes key immediately
   253→Providers: Phala Cloud (primary) / AWS Nitro (fallback)
   254→```
   255→
   256→## User Journey Example
   257→
   258→```text
   259→1. Signup (Google) → Web3Auth derives KeyA
   260→2. Upload file → Encrypt → IPFS CID → IPNS publish
   261→3. Phone login (Email) → Web3Auth derives KeyA (same!)
   262→4. Phone polls IPNS → Sees file → Downloads & decrypts
   263→5. Export vault → JSON with CIDs + encrypted root key
   264→6. CipherBox gone? → Use export + private key → Full recovery
   265→```
   266→
   267→## Further Reading
   268→
   269→- [Frozen Specifications](../00-Preliminary-R&D/Documentation/) — PRD, Technical Architecture, API Specification, Data Flows, Client Specification
   270→- [Authentication Architecture](AUTHENTICATION_ARCHITECTURE.md) — detailed auth flow documentation
   271→- [Metadata Schemas](METADATA_SCHEMAS.md) — all metadata object schemas with field tables
   272→- [Vault Export Format](VAULT_EXPORT_FORMAT.md) — export/recovery data format
   273→

    41→## Critical Architecture Patterns
    42→
    43→### Two-Phase Authentication Model
    44→
    45→CipherBox uses a **mandatory two-phase auth flow** that must be understood before implementing any auth-related features:
    46→
    47→1. **Phase 1 (Web3Auth):** User authenticates → Web3Auth derives ECDSA secp256k1 keypair via threshold cryptography
    48→2. **Phase 2 (CipherBox Backend):** Client authenticates with backend using either:
    49→   - **Option A:** Web3Auth ID token (JWT) validated via JWKS endpoint
    50→   - **Option B:** SIWE-like signature flow (nonce-based)
    51→
    52→**Key Insight:** The ECDSA keypair from Phase 1 is the user's identity. Web3Auth's "group connections" feature ensures that Google OAuth, email/password, magic links, and external wallet auth all derive the **same keypair** for the same user.
    53→
    54→### Zero-Knowledge Key Hierarchy
    55→
    56→```text
    57→User Auth → Web3Auth → ECDSA Private Key (client RAM only, never transmitted)
    58→                    ├─ Used for ECIES decryption of all data keys
    59→                    ├─ Used to decrypt IPNS signing keys (Ed25519)
    60→                    └─ Destroyed on logout
    61→
    62→ECDSA Public Key (stored on server, identifies user)
    63→    └─ Used to encrypt (ECIES):
    64→        ├─ Root Folder Key (AES-256, stored encrypted on server)
    65→        ├─ Subfolder Keys (AES-256, stored encrypted in parent IPNS metadata)
    66→        └─ File Keys (AES-256, stored encrypted in folder IPNS metadata)
    67→```
    68→
    69→**Critical Rule:** Never log, persist to disk, or transmit the ECDSA private key. It exists ONLY in client memory during the session.
    70→
    71→### Per-Folder IPNS Architecture
    72→
    73→Each folder has its own IPNS entry containing encrypted metadata. This design enables future per-folder sharing (v2+).
    74→
    75→**Folder Metadata Structure:**
    76→
    77→```typescript
    78→interface DecryptedFolderMetadata {
    79→  children: Array<{
    80→    type: 'file' | 'folder';
    81→    nameEncrypted: string; // AES-256-GCM(name, folderKey)
    82→    nameIv: string;
    83→    cid?: string; // For files: IPFS CID
    84→    ipnsName?: string; // For folders: IPNS name
    85→    fileKeyEncrypted?: string; // ECIES(fileKey, userPubkey)
    86→    subfolderKeyEncrypted?: string; // ECIES(folderKey, userPubkey)
    87→    size?: number;
    88→    created: number;
    89→    modified: number;
    90→  }>;
    91→}
    92→```
    93→
    94→**When modifying files/folders:** Always re-encrypt and republish the containing folder's IPNS entry.
    95→
    96→## Technology Stack & Standards
    97→
    98→### Encryption Primitives (Non-Negotiable)
    99→
   100→| Algorithm           | Use Case                            | Implementation                |
   101→| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
   102→| **AES-256-GCM**     | File content + metadata encryption  | Web Crypto API / libsodium.js |
   103→| **ECIES secp256k1** | Key wrapping (files, folders)       | ethers.js / libsodium.js      |
   104→| **ECDSA secp256k1** | IPNS signing, user identity         | Web3Auth / ethers.js          |
   105→| **HKDF-SHA256**     | Key derivation                      | Web Crypto API                |
   106→| **Argon2**          | Password hashing (server-side only) | argon2-browser                |
   107→
   108→**Never use:** Custom crypto, CBC mode, ECB mode, MD5, SHA1

   119→## Development Patterns
   120→
   121→### API Development Workflow
   122→
   123→When working on `apps/api` code:
   124→
   125→1. **After modifying API endpoints, DTOs, or controllers**, regenerate the API client to keep the web app in sync:
   126→
   127→   ```bash
   128→   pnpm api:generate
   129→   ```
   130→
   131→   This command generates the OpenAPI spec from the API, creates the typed client for the web app, and runs lint fixes.
   132→
   133→2. **Always run `pnpm api:generate` before completing a feature** that touches the API to ensure type safety across the monorepo.
   134→
   135→3. **Commit the regenerated client files** (`apps/web/src/api/`) along with your API changes.
   136→
   137→### File Upload Flow (Reference Implementation)
   138→
   139→```typescript
   140→// 1. Generate random file key
   141→const fileKey = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));
   142→const fileIV = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12)); // GCM uses 96-bit IV
   143→
   144→// 2. Encrypt file content
   145→const encryptedFile = await crypto.subtle.encrypt(
   146→  { name: 'AES-GCM', iv: fileIV },
   147→  await crypto.subtle.importKey('raw', fileKey, 'AES-GCM', false, ['encrypt']),
   148→  fileContent
   149→);
   150→
   151→// 3. Wrap file key with user's public key (ECIES)
   152→const encryptedFileKey = await eciesEncrypt(fileKey, userPublicKey);
   153→
   154→// 4. Upload encrypted file to backend → Pinata → get CID
   155→const { cid } = await api.post('/vault/upload', {
   156→  encryptedFile: new Blob([encryptedFile]),
   157→  fileName: file.name, // plaintext OK for server audit
   158→  iv: bytesToHex(fileIV),
   159→});
   160→
   161→// 5. Add to folder metadata (all encrypted)
   162→const fileEntry = {
   163→  type: 'file',
   164→  nameEncrypted: await aesEncrypt(file.name, folderKey),
   165→  nameIv: crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12)),
   166→  cid,
   167→  fileKeyEncrypted: encryptedFileKey,
   168→  fileIv: bytesToHex(fileIV),
   169→  size: file.size,
   170→  created: Date.now(),
   171→  modified: Date.now(),
   172→};
   173→
   174→// 6. Re-encrypt folder metadata and republish IPNS
   175→await republishFolderIPNS(folderId, updatedMetadata);
   176→```
   177→
   178→### IPNS Publishing Pattern
   179→
   180→Every write operation (create/rename/move/delete) must:
   181→
   182→1. Update the in-memory folder metadata
   183→2. Re-encrypt the entire metadata JSON with the folder key
   184→3. Sign the encrypted metadata with ECDSA private key
   185→4. Call `POST /vault/publish-ipns` with signed entry
   186→
   187→**Performance Note:** IPNS publishing is the bottleneck (~2s). Batch operations when possible (e.g., multi-file upload should publish once at the end).
   188→
   189→### Session Token Management
   190→
   191→```typescript
   192→// Access tokens (15min, memory only)
   193→const accessToken = response.data.accessToken;
   194→// Store in: React context / Zustand / Redux (never localStorage)
   195→
   196→// Refresh tokens (7 days, secure storage)
   197→const refreshToken = response.data.refreshToken;
   198→// Store in: HTTP-only cookie (preferred) OR encrypted localStorage
   199→
   200→// Token refresh pattern
   201→if (error.response?.status === 401) {
   202→  const newAccessToken = await refreshAccessToken();
   203→  // Retry original request with new token
   204→}
   205→```

   207→## Common Pitfalls & Anti-Patterns
   208→
   209→### ❌ Never Do This
   210→
   211→1. **Storing keys in plaintext localStorage**
   212→
   213→   ```typescript
   214→   // WRONG
   215→   localStorage.setItem('privateKey', privateKeyHex);
   216→   ```
   217→
   218→2. **Logging sensitive data**
   219→
   220→   ```typescript
   221→   // WRONG
   222→   console.log('User private key:', privateKey);
   223→   console.log('Decrypted file:', fileContent);
   224→   ```
   225→
   226→3. **Sending plaintext to server**
   227→
   228→   ```typescript
   229→   // WRONG
   230→   await api.post('/vault/upload', { fileContent: file });
   231→   ```
   232→
   233→4. **Using sync crypto in main thread**
   234→
   235→   ```typescript
   236→   // WRONG (blocks UI for large files)
   237→   const encrypted = aesEncryptSync(largeFile, key);
   238→   ```
   239→
   240→### ✅ Correct Patterns
   241→
   242→1. **Store keys in memory, clear on logout**
   243→
   244→   ```typescript
   245→   // React context for session-scoped state
   246→   const [ecdsaPrivateKey, setEcdsaPrivateKey] = useState<Uint8Array | null>(null);
   247→
   248→   const logout = () => {
   249→     setEcdsaPrivateKey(null); // Cleared from memory
   250→     // No disk persistence
   251→   };
   252→   ```
   253→
   254→2. **Use Web Workers for large file encryption**
   255→
   256→   ```typescript
   257→   const worker = new Worker('./crypto-worker.js');
   258→   worker.postMessage({ fileData, key });
   259→   worker.onmessage = (e) => {
   260→     const encrypted = e.data;
   261→   };
   262→   ```
   263→
   264→3. **Always validate IPNS signatures client-side**
   265→
   266→   ```typescript
   267→   const messageHash = await sha256(signedEntry.encryptedMetadata);
   268→   const isValid = await ecdsaVerify(messageHash, signedEntry.signature, userPubkey);
   269→   if (!isValid) throw new Error('Metadata tampering detected');
   270→   ```

     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→CipherBox is a production-grade, privacy-first encrypted cloud storage platform using IPFS/IPNS and Web3Auth. It provides zero-knowledge file storage with user-to-user sharing, link sharing, client-side search, multi-factor authentication, file versioning, conflict detection, recycle bin, and cross-platform desktop apps (macOS, Windows, Linux). The server is cryptographically unable to access user data.
     6→
     7→## Core Value
     8→
     9→**Zero-knowledge privacy**: Files are encrypted client-side before leaving the device, and encryption keys exist only in client memory. The server is cryptographically unable to access user data.

    86→## Context
    87→
    88→**Current State (v1.0 shipped 2026-03-05):**
    89→
    90→- 423,869 lines of TypeScript + Rust across 698 source files

    96→**Technical Environment:**
    97→
    98→- IPFS via Pinata for file storage and pinning
    99→- IPNS for mutable metadata pointers (per-folder + per-file)
   100→- Web3Auth Core Kit MPC for deterministic ECDSA key derivation

   103→**Key Architecture (evolved through M1 + M2):**
   104→
   105→- Client-side encryption only — server is zero-knowledge relay
   106→- Per-folder + per-file IPNS keypairs (HKDF-derived)

   108→- Optimistic concurrency on IPNS publishes (sequence number checks)

   121→- **IPFS provider**: Pinata — managed pinning service

   127→| Full-stack vertical build order             | Test features end-to-end as they're built                  | Good    |
   128→| Web + cross-platform desktop for v1.0       | Complete user experience across all platforms              | Good    |
   129→| TEE republishing required for v1.0          | Zero-downtime vault access guarantee                       | Good    |
   130→| Core Kit MPC replaces PnP Modal             | Self-hosted identity provider, MFA foundation              | Good    |
   131→| Per-file IPNS metadata split                | Decouple content updates from folder publishes             | Good    |
   132→| AES-256-CTR for streaming media             | Byte-range decryption enables in-browser playback          | Good    |
   133→| Optimistic concurrency via sequence numbers | Lightweight conflict detection without distributed locks   | Good    |

   135→| Encrypted recycle bin on IPFS               | Client-side retention enforcement, CID unpinning on delete | Good    |
   136→| SIWE wallet login with hashed identifiers   | Privacy-preserving auth, unified identity across methods   | Good    |
   137→| Decimal phase numbering for insertions      | Clear insertion semantics without renumbering              | Good    |

     3→title: Add bring-your-own IPFS node support
     4→area: api
     5→files:
     6→  - apps/api/src/ipfs/ipfs.module.ts
     7→  - apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/ipfs-provider.interface.ts
     8→  - apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/local.provider.ts
     9→  - apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/pinata.provider.ts
    10→  - apps/api/.env.example
    11→  - apps/web/src/lib/api/ipfs.ts
    12→---
    13→
    14→## Problem
    15→
    16→Currently CipherBox supports two IPFS providers: Pinata (production default) and a local Kubo node (dev/testing). Both are configured server-side via environment variables (`IPFS_PROVIDER`, `IPFS_LOCAL_API_URL`). There is no way for end users to bring their own IPFS node — the choice is made by the server operator, not the individual user.
    17→
    18→For a zero-knowledge privacy tool, users may want to:
    19→
    20→- Pin their encrypted data to their own IPFS node (self-sovereignty)
    21→- Use a preferred pinning service other than Pinata (e.g., web3.storage, Filebase, nft.storage)
    22→- Run a personal Kubo/IPFS node at home and have CipherBox pin directly to it
    23→- Avoid relying on a third-party pinning service entirely
    24→
    25→This requires a user-level IPFS configuration (not just server-level env vars) and potentially a hybrid model where the backend can relay uploads to a user-specified IPFS endpoint, or the client uploads directly to the user's node.
    26→
    27→## Solution
    28→
    29→TBD — key design questions to resolve:
    30→
    31→1. **Client-direct vs server-relay:** Should the web app upload encrypted blobs directly to the user's IPFS node (bypassing backend), or should the backend proxy to the user's configured endpoint?
    32→   - Client-direct: simpler, no server load, but CORS/connectivity issues
    33→   - Server-relay: consistent quota tracking, but server sees user's IPFS credentials
    34→
    35→2. **User settings model:** Add per-user IPFS config (endpoint URL, auth token, provider type) stored in user settings. UI for configuring custom node in settings page.
    36→
    37→3. **Provider abstraction:** The existing `IpfsProviderInterface` (pin/unpin/fetch) is already well-abstracted. A new "user-custom" provider that reads config from user settings rather than env vars would slot in cleanly.
    38→
    39→4. **IPNS implications:** If user pins to their own node, IPNS republishing and delegated routing need to work with the user's node or be handled differently.
    40→
    41→5. **Quota tracking:** If uploads go directly to user's node, server-side quota tracking becomes optional or advisory.
    42→
    43→6. **Fallback/reliability:** What happens if user's node is unreachable? Fallback to default provider, or fail?
    44→
    45→7. **Conflict detection:** Phase 16 (M2) adds API-level optimistic concurrency for conflict detection — the API checks IPNS sequence numbers on publish. BYO-IPFS bypasses the API for publishes, so this conflict detection mechanism will stop working. This feature will need a client-side conflict detection strategy (e.g., IPNS resolution before publish, or CRDT-based metadata) when BYO-IPFS is implemented.
    46→

    24→
    25→## 1. Existing Architecture Summary
    26→
    27→Before detailing M3 additions, here is the current system as of M1/M2 completion.
    28→
    29→### Current Components
    30→
    31→| Component | Technology                    | Role                                           |
    32→| --------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
    33→| Web App   | React 18 + Zustand + Vite     | File browser, auth, upload/download, IPNS sync |
    34→| API       | NestJS + TypeORM + PostgreSQL | Auth, vault, IPFS/IPNS relay, TEE coordination |
    35→| Desktop   | Tauri v2 + Rust FUSE          | Transparent encrypted filesystem mount         |
    36→| IPFS      | Pinata (managed pinning)      | Encrypted content storage                      |
    37→| IPNS      | Per-folder Ed25519 keypairs   | Mutable metadata pointers                      |
    38→| TEE       | Phala Cloud / AWS Nitro       | IPNS auto-republishing                         |
    39→| Auth      | Web3Auth + SIWE               | Key derivation and identity                    |
    40→
    41→### Key Constraints Preserved in M3
    42→
    43→1. **Zero-knowledge server** -- the backend NEVER sees plaintext content or unencrypted keys
    44→2. **Client-side encryption** -- all crypto operations happen in-browser or in-desktop
    45→3. **Per-folder IPNS** -- each folder has its own Ed25519 keypair and AES-256 folder key
    46→4. **ECIES key wrapping** -- all symmetric keys wrapped with user's secp256k1 public key
    47→
    48→### By M3, These M2 Features Exist
    49→
    50→- File/folder sharing via ECIES re-wrapping (shared folder keys re-encrypted to recipient's public key)
    51→- File versioning (version chains stored in folder metadata)
    52→- Client-side search (encrypted index)
    53→- MFA support
    54→
    55→---
    56→
    57→## 2. Document Editors
    58→
    59→### 2.1 Problem Statement
    60→
    61→CipherBox stores encrypted files on IPFS. Currently, editing requires download, decrypt, edit in external app, re-encrypt, re-upload. M3 adds in-browser editing for documents, spreadsheets, and presentations -- while preserving zero-knowledge.
    62→
    63→### 2.2 Architecture Decision: Decrypt-Edit-Encrypt Pipeline
    64→
    65→The fundamental pattern for all editors is:
    66→
    67→```text
    68→1. User opens file in CipherBox
    69→2. Client fetches encrypted blob from IPFS via backend relay
    70→3. Client decrypts with file's AES-256-GCM key
    71→4. Decrypted content loaded into in-browser editor component
    72→5. User edits in the editor (all in-browser, all in RAM)
    73→6. On save: editor exports content -> client encrypts -> uploads to IPFS -> updates IPNS metadata
    74→7. Old CID unpinned
    75→```
    76→
    77→This is architecturally identical to the existing "update file" flow (DATA_FLOWS.md section 6.5) but with the editor replacing the download/re-upload step.
    78→
    79→### 2.3 Editor Technology Recommendations
    80→
    81→#### Rich Text / Documents: Tiptap (built on ProseMirror)
    82→
    83→Recommended editor: TipTap 3.x
    84→
    85→| Criterion             | Tiptap                        | CKEditor 5               | Quill               |
    86→| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------- |
    87→| React integration     | Native (@tiptap/react)        | Adapter needed           | React-Quill wrapper |
    88→| Content format        | JSON (ProseMirror doc)        | Custom model             | Delta JSON          |
    89→| Headless / unstyled   | Yes (matches existing UI)     | No (opinionated UI)      | Partial             |
    90→| Collaboration support | Yjs plugin (optional, future) | Proprietary              | Limited             |
    91→| License               | MIT (core)                    | GPL (open) or commercial | BSD                 |
    92→| Bundle size           | Modular, ~50KB base           | ~300KB+                  | ~40KB               |
    93→
    94→**Why Tiptap:**
    95→
    96→- Headless architecture -- CipherBox can style the editor to match existing UI
    97→- JSON export via `editor.getJSON()` maps cleanly to encrypt-and-store
    98→- ProseMirror schema enforcement prevents invalid document structures
    99→- Yjs integration available for future real-time collaboration (M4+)
   100→- MIT licensed core is compatible with CipherBox
   101→
   102→**Content format:** Tiptap's ProseMirror JSON document is the "file format" for CipherBox documents. This JSON is what gets AES-256-GCM encrypted and stored on IPFS.
   103→
   104→```typescript
   105→// Save flow (simplified)
   106→const docJson = editor.getJSON();
   107→const plaintext = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(docJson));
   108→const fileKey = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32));
   109→const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
   110→const ciphertext = await aesGcmEncrypt(plaintext, fileKey, iv);
   111→// Upload ciphertext to IPFS, wrap fileKey with ECIES, update IPNS
   112→```
   113→
   114→#### Spreadsheets: Univer
   115→
   116→Recommended editor: Univer (successor to Luckysheet)
   117→
   118→| Criterion           | Univer              | Handsontable            | SheetJS           |
   119→| ------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------- |
   120→| Full spreadsheet UI | Yes                 | Yes                     | No (parsing only) |
   121→| React integration   | Official plugin     | Yes                     | N/A               |
   122→| Formulas            | 400+ Excel formulas | Limited                 | Parsing only      |
   123→| License             | Apache 2.0          | Commercial (CE limited) | Apache 2.0        |
   124→| Client-side only    | Yes                 | Yes                     | Yes               |
   125→| Import/export       | XLSX, CSV           | CSV                     | XLSX, CSV, ODS    |
   126→
   127→**Why Univer:**
   128→
   129→- Full-featured Excel-like editor that runs entirely client-side
   130→- Apache 2.0 license
   131→- Successor to Luckysheet with active development
   132→- Supports React embedding
   133→- Exports to JSON model that can be encrypted
   134→
   135→**Content format:** Univer's workbook model (JSON) is encrypted and stored on IPFS. XLSX import/export happens client-side for interoperability.
   136→
   137→#### Presentations: Defer to M4
   138→
   139→Recommended approach: Defer slide editing to a later milestone.
   140→
   141→Rationale:
   142→
   143→- No mature, embeddable, client-side-only presentation WYSIWYG editor exists in the open-source ecosystem
   144→- Reveal.js is a presentation renderer, not an editor
   145→- OnlyOffice has a presentation editor but requires a server-side Document Server (violates zero-knowledge)
   146→- Building a custom slide editor is a multi-month effort
   147→- Documents and spreadsheets cover 90% of productivity use cases
   148→
   149→For M3, presentation files (.pptx) can still be stored/shared as encrypted files -- just not edited in-browser.
   150→
   151→### 2.4 New File Types in Metadata
   152→
   153→Folder metadata `children` entries gain a new field:
   154→
   155→```typescript
   156→// Existing file entry (unchanged)
   157→type FileEntry = {
   158→  type: 'file';
   159→  nameEncrypted: string;
   160→  nameIv: string;
   161→  cid: string;
   162→  fileKeyEncrypted: string;
   163→  fileIv: string;
   164→  encryptionMode: 'GCM' | 'CTR';
   165→  size: number;
   166→  // NEW: editor type hint
   167→  editorType?: 'document' | 'spreadsheet' | 'text' | 'image';
   168→  // NEW: native format for editor content
   169→  editorFormat?: 'tiptap-json' | 'univer-json' | 'plaintext';
   170→  created: number;
   171→  modified: number;
   172→};
   173→```
   174→
   175→**Important:** `editorType` and `editorFormat` are stored in encrypted metadata (inside the AES-GCM-encrypted folder metadata). The server never sees them.
   176→
   177→### 2.5 Integration Points with Existing Components
   178→
   179→| Existing Component                                           | Change Required                                    |
   180→| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
   181→| `apps/web/src/services/file-crypto.service.ts`               | Add editor content serialization/deserialization   |
   182→| `apps/web/src/services/download.service.ts`                  | Add "open in editor" path alongside download       |
   183→| `apps/web/src/services/upload.service.ts`                    | Add "save from editor" path alongside file upload  |
   184→| `apps/web/src/stores/folder.store.ts`                        | Surface `editorType` for routing to correct editor |
   185→| `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/FileListItem.tsx`      | Add "Edit" action for editable types               |
   186→| New: `apps/web/src/components/editors/DocumentEditor.tsx`    | Tiptap editor wrapper                              |
   187→| New: `apps/web/src/components/editors/SpreadsheetEditor.tsx` | Univer editor wrapper                              |
   188→| New: `apps/web/src/services/editor.service.ts`               | Decrypt-edit-encrypt pipeline orchestration        |
   189→| New: `apps/web/src/stores/editor.store.ts`                   | Editor state (dirty flag, autosave timer)          |
   190→
   191→### 2.6 Autosave Strategy
   192→
   193→Since saving involves re-encrypting and re-uploading to IPFS (not trivially cheap), autosave should be debounced:
   194→
   195→- Autosave interval: 60 seconds after last edit (configurable)
   196→- Manual save: always available
   197→- Dirty indicator: shown when unsaved changes exist
   198→- On close with unsaved changes: confirm dialog
   199→- Each save creates a new CID (by design -- IPFS is append-only)

   203→## 3. Team Accounts
   204→
   205→### 3.1 Architecture Decision: Shared Team Vaults with Per-Team Key Hierarchy
   206→
   207→Following the patterns established by Keeper and Bitwarden for zero-knowledge team vaults.
   208→
   209→### 3.2 Key Hierarchy Extension
   210→
   211→Current key hierarchy (per-user):
   212→
   213→```text
   214→User ECDSA Keypair (secp256k1)
   215→  -> rootFolderKey (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   216→    -> folderKey per folder (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   217→      -> fileKey per file (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to user's publicKey)
   218→```
   219→
   220→Extended hierarchy for teams:
   221→
   222→```text
   223→Team
   224→  -> teamKey (AES-256, randomly generated on team creation)
   225→    -> teamFolderKey per shared folder (AES-256, ECIES-wrapped to... what?)
   226→
   227→Each team member gets:
   228→  -> encryptedTeamKey = ECIES(teamKey, memberPublicKey)
   229→    stored in team_members table
   230→```
   231→
   232→**How it works:**
   233→
   234→1. Team creator generates a random `teamKey` (AES-256)
   235→2. Creator encrypts `teamKey` with their own `publicKey` and stores it
   236→3. When inviting a member, creator decrypts `teamKey` client-side, then re-encrypts with invitee's `publicKey`
   237→4. Team folders use `teamKey` as the root -- subfolder keys and file keys within team folders are ECIES-wrapped to each member's `publicKey` OR encrypted with `teamKey`
   238→
   239→#### Design Decision: Wrap to teamKey, Not Individual publicKeys
   240→
   241→For team folders, file keys and folder keys should be encrypted with the `teamKey` rather than individual member public keys. This means:
   242→
   243→- Adding a team member = re-encrypt `teamKey` to their public key (one operation)
   244→- Removing a team member = rotate `teamKey` and re-encrypt to remaining members (heavier, but necessary for security)
   245→- Files in team folders encrypted with keys derived from `teamKey`, not per-member
   246→
   247→This matches the Keeper/Bitwarden model and avoids the O(members x files) key re-wrapping problem.
   248→
   249→### 3.3 Permission Model
   250→
   251→```typescript
   252→type TeamRole = 'owner' | 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
   253→
   254→// Capabilities per role
   255→const ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
   256→  owner: ['read', 'write', 'delete', 'manage_members', 'manage_team', 'billing'],
   257→  admin: ['read', 'write', 'delete', 'manage_members'],
   258→  editor: ['read', 'write'],
   259→  viewer: ['read'],
   260→} as const;
   261→```
   262→
   263→**Permission enforcement:**
   264→
   265→- **Server-side:** Team membership and role checked on all team-scoped API calls
   266→- **Client-side:** UI hides actions the user's role does not permit
   267→- **Crypto-level:** Viewers receive `teamKey` (read access means decrypt access -- cannot be revoked cryptographically without key rotation)
   268→
   269→**Important caveat:** In a zero-knowledge system, read access = possession of decryption key. A viewer who has been removed can still decrypt previously-accessed content. Revoking access requires rotating the `teamKey` and re-encrypting all team folder content. This is an inherent limitation of client-side encryption architectures.
   270→
   271→### 3.4 Team IPNS Architecture
   272→
   273→Team folders need their own IPNS keypairs, just like user folders. The difference is the IPNS private key management:
   274→
   275→- Team folder's `ipnsPrivateKey` is encrypted with `teamKey` (not individual member's public key)
   276→- Any team member with `editor` or higher role can decrypt `teamKey`, then decrypt `ipnsPrivateKey`, then sign IPNS updates
   277→- TEE republishing for team folders: `encryptedIpnsPrivateKey` is still encrypted with TEE public key (unchanged)
   278→

   482→## 5. Document Signing
   483→
   484→### 5.1 Architecture Decision: Cryptographic Signatures with CipherBox Keys
   485→
   486→CipherBox users already have secp256k1 ECDSA keypairs (from Web3Auth). These can produce digital signatures that are cryptographically verifiable. However, these are NOT legally binding qualified electronic signatures (QES) under eIDAS without certificate authority backing.
   487→
   488→### 5.2 Signature Levels
   489→
   490→| Level                                | CipherBox Support                                                                      | Legal Standing                            |
   491→| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
   492→| Simple Electronic Signature (SES)    | Yes -- intent captured, signature stored                                               | Legally recognized in most jurisdictions  |
   493→| Advanced Electronic Signature (AES)  | Partially -- uniquely linked to signer via secp256k1 key, but no qualified certificate | Recognized with higher evidentiary value  |
   494→| Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) | No -- requires qualified certificate from QTSP                                         | Equivalent to handwritten signature in EU |
   495→
   496→**Recommendation for M3:** Implement SES/AES-level signing using existing secp256k1 keys. QES requires integration with a Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) and is out of scope for a technology demonstrator.
   497→
   498→### 5.3 Signing Flow
   499→
   500→```text
   501→1. User opens document to sign
   502→2. Client decrypts document content
   503→3. Client computes SHA-256 hash of plaintext content
   504→4. Client signs hash with user's secp256k1 privateKey:
   505→   signature = ECDSA_sign(SHA256(content), privateKey)
   506→5. Signature metadata stored in folder metadata alongside file entry:
   507→   {
   508→     signerPublicKey: "0x04abc...",
   509→     signatureHex: "0xdef...",
   510→     contentHash: "sha256:abc123...",
   511→     signedAt: 1707000000,
   512→     signedCid: "QmXxx..."  // CID of the content that was signed
   513→   }
   514→6. Signature metadata encrypted with folderKey (part of IPNS metadata)
   515→7. Verification: any user with folder access can verify signature
   516→   matches publicKey and content hash
   517→```
   518→
   519→### 5.4 Verification Properties
   520→
   521→- **Integrity:** SHA-256 content hash ensures signed content has not been modified
   522→- **Non-repudiation:** ECDSA signature proves the holder of the private key signed
   523→- **Timestamp:** `signedAt` provides temporal evidence (not cryptographic timestamp -- would need TSA for that)
   524→- **Auditability:** The `signedCid` links the signature to a specific IPFS CID
   525→
   526→### 5.5 Multi-Signer Support
   527→
   528→For documents requiring multiple signatures (e.g., contracts):
   529→
   530→```typescript
   531→type SignatureRecord = {
   532→  signerPublicKey: string;
   533→  signatureHex: string;
   534→  contentHash: string;
   535→  signedAt: number;
   536→  signedCid: string;
   537→};
   538→
   539→// In file entry metadata
   540→type SignableFileEntry = FileEntry & {
   541→  signatures?: SignatureRecord[];
   542→  requiredSigners?: string[]; // publicKeys of required signers
   543→  signatureStatus?: 'pending' | 'partial' | 'complete';
   544→};
   545→```
   546→
   547→### 5.6 Integration Points
   548→
   549→| Existing Component                                         | Change                                 |
   550→| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
   551→| Folder metadata schema                                     | Add `signatures` array to file entries |
   552→| `apps/web/src/services/file-crypto.service.ts`             | Add signing and verification functions |
   553→| `apps/web/src/components/file-browser/FileListItem.tsx`    | Show signature status icon             |
   554→| New: `apps/web/src/components/signing/SignaturePanel.tsx`  | UI for signing and viewing signatures  |
   555→| New: `apps/web/src/components/signing/VerifySignature.tsx` | Verification results display           |
   556→| New: `apps/web/src/services/signing.service.ts`            | ECDSA signing/verification logic       |
   557→
   558→### 5.7 What This Is NOT
   559→
   560→- NOT a replacement for DocuSign/Adobe Sign (no legal compliance framework)
   561→- NOT QES (no qualified certificates)
   562→- NOT timestamped by a TSA (trusted timestamping authority)
   563→- IS a cryptographic proof that a specific key holder approved specific content at a claimed time
   564→- IS verifiable by any party with the signer's public key

   741→## 9. Real-Time Collaboration Assessment
   742→
   743→### 9.1 Verdict: Defer Real-Time Collaboration to M4+
   744→
   745→Real-time collaborative editing with end-to-end encryption is a hard problem. Here is why it should be deferred:
   746→
   747→### 9.2 Technical Challenges
   748→
   749→1. **Encrypted CRDTs:** Standard CRDT implementations (Yjs, Automerge) assume a trusted relay server. For zero-knowledge, updates must be encrypted before transmission. CryptPad solved this with custom encrypted operational transforms, but it took years of development.
   750→
   751→2. **Key distribution for real-time:** Every CRDT update needs to be encrypted. Broadcasting encrypted deltas to N users requires either:
   752→   - Encrypt once with shared key (team key approach -- feasible but requires all participants to have key)
   753→   - Encrypt N times for N participants (O(N) per keystroke -- not scalable)
   754→
   755→3. **Presence and cursors:** Showing other users' cursor positions requires some form of real-time channel. This could be done without compromising zero-knowledge (encrypted WebSocket messages), but adds significant infrastructure.
   756→
   757→4. **Conflict resolution with encryption:** CRDT merge operations need to operate on plaintext. In a zero-knowledge system, the server cannot merge -- all merging must happen client-side, which means every client needs every other client's updates decrypted.
   758→
   759→5. **Infrastructure:** Requires WebSocket server for real-time messaging (not currently in the architecture).
   760→
   761→### 9.3 What M3 Should Build Instead
   762→
   763→Single-user editing with conflict detection:
   764→
   765→- User opens document for editing (acquires soft lock)
   766→- If another user opens same document, they see "Currently being edited by [user]"
   767→- Second user can choose to open read-only or force-edit (last-write-wins)
   768→- Lock released on save or close (with timeout fallback)
   769→
   770→This is the same model used by SharePoint's "check-out" feature and is pragmatic for a technology demonstrator.
   771→
   772→### 9.4 Lock Implementation
   773→
   774→```typescript
   775→// Lock stored in team vault metadata (encrypted)
   776→type DocumentLock = {
   777→  lockedBy: string; // publicKey of lock holder
   778→  lockedAt: number; // timestamp
   779→  lockTimeout: number; // auto-release after N seconds (default: 3600)
   780→};
   781→```
   782→
   783→Since locks are in IPNS metadata (encrypted), they are eventually consistent (30s polling). This is acceptable for the advisory lock pattern.

    41→## Feature 1: File/Folder Sharing (Zero-Knowledge Key Exchange)
    42→
    43→### Architecture Decision
    44→
    45→Sharing in a zero-knowledge system requires the **sender to re-encrypt keys for the recipient's public key**. CipherBox already wraps every key (folderKey, fileKey, ipnsPrivateKey) with ECIES using the owner's publicKey. Sharing means producing additional ECIES-wrapped copies of those keys for each recipient's publicKey.
    46→
    47→No new cryptographic library is needed. The existing `eciesjs` (already `^0.4.16`) handles all required ECIES operations. The `wrapKey()` function in `packages/crypto/src/ecies/encrypt.ts` already accepts any recipient publicKey.
    48→
    49→### New Dependencies: NONE for crypto
    50→
    51→The sharing protocol is purely a server-side coordination + client-side key re-wrapping exercise.
    52→
    53→### Server-Side Additions
    54→
    55→| Need                          | Solution                                          | New Dependency?            |
    56→| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
    57→| Share invitation records      | New TypeORM entities (`Share`, `ShareInvitation`) | No -- use existing TypeORM |
    58→| Recipient public key lookup   | New API endpoint `/users/lookup?publicKey=0x...`  | No                         |
    59→| Share token generation        | Use existing `jose` for signed share tokens       | No                         |
    60→| Permission model (read/write) | Metadata field in `Share` entity                  | No                         |
    61→| Notification of new shares    | BullMQ job (already have queue infrastructure)    | No                         |
    62→

    65→| Need                                    | Solution                                          | New Dependency? |
    66→| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    67→| Re-encrypt folderKey for recipient      | Existing `wrapKey(folderKey, recipientPublicKey)` | No              |
    68→| Re-encrypt ipnsPrivateKey for recipient | Same `wrapKey()`                                  | No              |

    85→## Feature 2: Client-Side Encrypted Search Index
    86→
    87→### The Zero-Knowledge Constraint
    88→
    89→The server MUST NOT know what the user is searching for or what the search results are. This eliminates all server-side search solutions (Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL full-text search, etc.).
    90→
    91→The search index must be:
    92→
    93→1. **Built client-side** from decrypted file/folder names and metadata
    94→2. **Stored client-side** (encrypted at rest in IndexedDB)
    95→3. **Queried client-side** in the browser/desktop
    96→
    97→### Recommended: MiniSearch
    98→
    99→| Library    | Version | Weekly Downloads | TypeScript         | Zero-Dep | Size       |
   100→| ---------- | ------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | -------- | ---------- |
   101→| MiniSearch | ^7.2.0  | ~700K            | Native (src in TS) | Yes      | ~7KB gzip  |
   102→| Fuse.js    | ^7.0.0  | ~5M              | Types included     | Yes      | ~15KB gzip |
   103→| FlexSearch | ^0.7.43 | ~420K            | Community types    | Yes      | ~6KB gzip  |
   104→| Lunr       | ^2.3.9  | ~3.7M            | Community types    | Yes      | ~8KB gzip  |
   105→
   106→Why MiniSearch over alternatives:
   107→
   108→1. **Written in TypeScript natively** (since v7.0.0) -- not just type declarations bolted on, but full TypeScript source. Aligns with project standards.
   109→2. **Supports index serialization/deserialization** -- Critical for persisting the encrypted index to IndexedDB. `JSON.stringify(miniSearch)` produces a serializable index that can be encrypted with AES-256-GCM and stored.
   110→3. **Prefix search + fuzzy search + field boosting** -- Covers all search UX needs for filename/path matching.
   111→4. **Zero runtime dependencies** -- No supply chain risk.
   112→5. **Memory efficient** -- Designed for browser environments and mobile-constrained memory.
   113→
   114→Why NOT Fuse.js: Fuse.js is purely a fuzzy matcher -- it re-scans the full document list on every query (O(n)). MiniSearch builds an inverted index (O(log n) queries). For a vault with thousands of files, MiniSearch is materially faster.
   115→
   116→Why NOT FlexSearch: FlexSearch has stale TypeScript types (@types/flexsearch is unmaintained) and the v0.7.x API has breaking changes with poor migration docs. Its index serialization story is more complex.
   117→
   118→### Index Persistence Layer: idb (IndexedDB wrapper)
   119→
   120→| Library | Version | Purpose                         |
   121→| ------- | ------- | ------------------------------- |
   122→| `idb`   | ^8.0.0  | Promise-based IndexedDB wrapper |
   123→
   124→Why `idb` over `idb-keyval`: The search index needs object stores with structured queries (e.g., "get all index chunks"), not just key-value. `idb` (~1KB) provides the full IndexedDB API with promises. `idb-keyval` is simpler but insufficient.
   125→
   126→Why NOT localForage: Adds unnecessary abstraction and fallback logic (localStorage, WebSQL) that we don't need.

   129→
   130→```text
   131→Decrypted metadata (in memory)
   132→       |
   133→       v
   134→MiniSearch.addAll(documents)   <-- Build index from file names, paths, sizes, dates
   135→       |
   136→       v
   137→JSON.stringify(miniSearch)     <-- Serialize index
   138→       |
   139→       v
   140→AES-256-GCM encrypt            <-- Existing @cipherbox/crypto
   141→       |
   142→       v
   143→idb.put('search-index', encrypted)  <-- Persist to IndexedDB
   144→```

   146→On next session:

   153→       |
   154→       v
   155→MiniSearch.loadJSON(parsed)    <-- Restore index
   156→       |
   157→       v

   186→## Feature 3: MFA (Passkey/WebAuthn, TOTP, Recovery Phrase)
   187→
   188→### Two Layers of MFA
   189→
   190→CipherBox has a unique MFA architecture because authentication happens in two phases:
   191→
   192→1. **Web3Auth MFA** -- Protects the key derivation step (getting the ECDSA keypair)
   193→2. **CipherBox Backend MFA** -- Protects API access (optional additional layer)
   194→
   195→The PRD specifies MFA, and Web3Auth provides this natively. The recommended approach is to leverage Web3Auth's built-in MFA rather than building a separate MFA system.
   196→
   197→### Layer 1: Web3Auth Built-In MFA (PRIMARY)
   198→
   199→No new packages needed. The existing `@web3auth/modal` ^10.13.1 supports MFA configuration natively.
   200→
   201→Available factors (configured via `mfaSettings`):
   202→
   203→| Factor        | Config Key            | Description                        |
   204→| ------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
   205→| Device Share  | `deviceShareFactor`   | Stores a key share on the device   |
   206→| Backup Phrase | `backUpShareFactor`   | 24-word seed phrase for recovery   |
   207→| Social Backup | `socialBackupFactor`  | Backup via social login            |
   208→| Password      | `passwordFactor`      | User-chosen password               |
   209→| Passkeys      | `passkeysFactor`      | WebAuthn passkey                   |
   210→| Authenticator | `authenticatorFactor` | TOTP (Google Authenticator, Authy) |
   211→
   212→Configuration:
   213→
   214→```typescript
   215→const web3auth = new Web3Auth({
   216→  // ... existing config
   217→  mfaSettings: {
   218→    deviceShareFactor: { enable: true, priority: 1, mandatory: true },
   219→    backUpShareFactor: { enable: true, priority: 2, mandatory: true },
   220→    passkeysFactor: { enable: true, priority: 3, mandatory: false },
   221→    authenticatorFactor: { enable: true, priority: 4, mandatory: false },
   222→    passwordFactor: { enable: false },
   223→    socialBackupFactor: { enable: false },
   224→  },
   225→});
   226→```
   227→
   228→IMPORTANT CAVEAT: The `mfaSettings` configuration is a paid feature on Web3Auth's SCALE Plan. Verify current pricing before committing to this approach. On the `sapphire_devnet` network (which CipherBox likely uses for development), it is free.
   229→
   230→### Layer 2: CipherBox Backend WebAuthn (SECONDARY -- for API access)
   231→
   232→If the project wants WebAuthn passkeys as an additional factor for CipherBox API authentication (beyond Web3Auth), use `@simplewebauthn/*`.
   233→
   234→### Recommended: @simplewebauthn
   235→
   236→| Package                   | Version | Purpose                              | Where      |
   237→| ------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------- |
   238→| `@simplewebauthn/server`  | ^13.2.2 | Registration/verification on backend | `apps/api` |
   239→| `@simplewebauthn/browser` | ^13.2.2 | Browser WebAuthn API calls           | `apps/web` |
   240→
   241→Why @simplewebauthn:
   242→
   243→1. **TypeScript-first** -- 100% TypeScript source, excellent types
   244→2. **Most popular WebAuthn library for Node.js** -- 184 dependents for server, 284 for browser
   245→3. **Works with NestJS** -- Via `passport-simple-webauthn` or direct integration (no passport needed)
   246→4. **Actively maintained** -- v13.2.2 published October 2025
   247→5. **Handles complexity** -- WebAuthn has many edge cases (attestation formats, authenticator types, CBOR parsing). This library handles them all.
   248→
   249→NestJS Integration Pattern:
   250→
   251→Do NOT use `passport-simple-webauthn` (v0.1.0, 2 years stale). Instead, integrate `@simplewebauthn/server` directly into NestJS services:

   267→| Package   | Version | Purpose                    | Where                                            |
   268→| --------- | ------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
   269→| `otpauth` | ^9.5.0  | TOTP generation/validation | `apps/api` (generation), `apps/web` (QR display) |
   270→
   271→Why `otpauth` over `otplib`:
   272→
   273→1. **Zero dependencies** -- `otplib` v13 has dependencies; `otpauth` v9 is self-contained
   274→2. **Multi-runtime** -- Works in Node.js, Deno, Bun, and browsers
   275→3. **RFC compliant** -- RFC 4226 (HOTP), RFC 6238 (TOTP)
   276→4. **Key URI format** -- Built-in `otpauth://` URI generation for QR codes
   277→5. **Actively maintained** -- v9.5.0 published February 2026
   278→
   279→### Recovery Phrase
   280→
   281→No new library needed. Recovery phrase generation uses existing crypto primitives:
   282→
   283→- Generate 256 bits of entropy via `crypto.getRandomValues()`
   284→- Convert to BIP-39 mnemonic using `@noble/hashes` (SHA-256 for checksum) plus a wordlist
   285→- OR use Web3Auth's built-in `backUpShareFactor` which handles this automatically
   286→
   287→If implementing independently (outside Web3Auth), consider:
   288→
   289→| Package        | Version | Purpose                                              |
   290→| -------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
   291→| `@scure/bip39` | ^1.4.0  | BIP-39 mnemonic generation (from `@noble` ecosystem) |
   292→
   293→Why `@scure/bip39`: Same author as `@noble/*` libraries (Paul Miller), audited, zero dependencies, TypeScript-native.
   294→
   295→### Recommended MFA Strategy
   296→
   297→Use Web3Auth's built-in MFA as the primary mechanism. It protects the most critical step (key derivation). Adding CipherBox-level WebAuthn/TOTP is optional hardening for API access.
   298→
   299→| Factor           | Provider              | Priority      | Package                                |
   300→| ---------------- | --------------------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------- |
   301→| Device share     | Web3Auth              | 1 (mandatory) | `@web3auth/modal` (existing)           |
   302→| Backup phrase    | Web3Auth              | 2 (mandatory) | `@web3auth/modal` (existing)           |
   303→| Passkey/WebAuthn | Web3Auth OR CipherBox | 3 (optional)  | `@simplewebauthn/*` if CipherBox-level |
   304→| TOTP             | Web3Auth OR CipherBox | 4 (optional)  | `otpauth` if CipherBox-level           |
   305→
   306→### New Dependencies (if implementing CipherBox-level MFA beyond Web3Auth)
   307→
   308→```bash
   309→# Backend
   310→cd apps/api && pnpm add @simplewebauthn/server otpauth
   311→
   312→# Frontend
   313→cd apps/web && pnpm add @simplewebauthn/browser
   314→
   315→# Crypto (if custom recovery phrase)
   316→cd packages/crypto && pnpm add @scure/bip39
   317→```
   318→
   319→### Database Additions
   320→
   321→New TypeORM entities needed for CipherBox-level MFA:
   322→
   323→- `webauthn_credentials` -- Store WebAuthn credential IDs, public keys, counter, transports
   324→- `totp_secrets` -- Store encrypted TOTP secrets (encrypt with user's publicKey before storing)
   325→- `recovery_codes` -- Store hashed recovery codes (use `argon2`, already installed)
   326→
   327→### Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH
   328→
   329→Web3Auth MFA is well-documented but the `mfaSettings` is a paid feature (SCALE plan). SimpleWebAuthn v13 is mature. The open question is whether to implement MFA at the Web3Auth level, CipherBox level, or both. Recommend: Web3Auth level first, CipherBox level as optional hardening.

   332→
   333→## Feature 4: File Version History
   334→
   335→### IPFS Natural Fit
   336→
   337→IPFS is content-addressable -- every version of a file inherently has a different CID. The challenge is not storing versions (IPFS does this) but **tracking the version chain** (linking CIDs into a history).
   338→
   339→### Architecture: Version Chain in Metadata
   340→
   341→No new library needed. Version history is a metadata design problem, not a library problem.
   342→
   343→Extend the `FileEntry` type in `packages/crypto/src/folder/types.ts`:
   344→
   345→```typescript
   346→export type FileEntry = {
   347→  // ... existing fields
   348→  type: 'file';
   349→  id: string;
   350→  name: string;
   351→  cid: string;
   352→  fileKeyEncrypted: string;
   353→  fileIv: string;
   354→  encryptionMode: 'GCM';
   355→  size: number;
   356→  createdAt: number;
   357→  modifiedAt: number;
   358→
   359→  // NEW: Version history
   360→  /** Previous version CID chain (most recent first, capped) */
   361→  previousVersions?: FileVersionEntry[];
   362→  /** Current version number (starts at 1) */
   363→  versionNumber?: number;
   364→};
   365→
   366→export type FileVersionEntry = {
   367→  /** IPFS CID of this version */
   368→  cid: string;
   369→  /** ECIES-wrapped file key for this version */
   370→  fileKeyEncrypted: string;
   371→  /** IV used for this version */
   372→  fileIv: string;
   373→  /** File size at this version */
   374→  size: number;
   375→  /** When this version was created */
   376→  createdAt: number;
   377→  /** Version number */
   378→  versionNumber: number;
   379→};
   380→```
   381→
   382→### Version Retention Strategy
   383→
   384→Since file versions are pinned on IPFS (via Pinata), they consume storage quota. Need a configurable retention policy:
   385→
   386→| Strategy             | Implementation                                             |
   387→| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
   388→| Keep last N versions | `previousVersions.slice(0, N)` in metadata, unpin old CIDs |
   389→| Time-based retention | Filter `previousVersions` by `createdAt` threshold         |
   390→| Storage-based limit  | Track total version bytes, evict oldest when threshold hit |
   391→
   392→### Server-Side Support
   393→
   394→| Need                          | Solution                                   | New Dependency? |
   395→| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------- |
   396→| Track pinned version CIDs     | Extend existing `pinned_cids` entity       | No              |
   397→| Unpinning old versions        | BullMQ job to unpin expired version CIDs   | No              |
   398→| Version count limits per user | Config in vault settings                   | No              |
   399→| Storage quota accounting      | Include version bytes in quota calculation | No              |
   400→
   401→### What NOT to Build
   402→
   403→| Approach                  | Why Not                                                               |
   404→| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   405→| Git-like delta storage    | Over-engineered for file storage; IPFS is already content-addressable |
   406→| Separate version database | Violates zero-knowledge (server would know version relationships)     |
   407→| IPFS MFS versioning       | Deprecated/experimental; CipherBox doesn't use MFS                    |
   408→| IPVC / IPVFS              | Unmaintained projects, not suited for encrypted use case              |
   409→
   410→### New Dependencies: NONE
   411→
   412→### Confidence: HIGH
   413→
   414→Version history is purely a metadata schema extension plus Pinata pin management. The existing stack handles everything needed.

   418→## Feature 5: Advanced Sync (Conflict Resolution, Offline Queue, Selective Sync)
   419→
   420→### Current State
   421→
   422→CipherBox v1 uses IPNS polling (30s interval) with last-writer-wins based on IPNS sequence numbers. This is fragile under concurrent edits.
   423→
   424→### Conflict Resolution Strategy
   425→
   426→Recommendation: Do NOT adopt a full CRDT library. CipherBox's data model (encrypted file metadata in IPNS records) is fundamentally different from collaborative text editing. CRDTs like Yjs/Automerge are designed for real-time co-editing of shared data structures -- overkill for file metadata sync.
   427→
   428→Instead, implement Operational Transform (OT) at the metadata level:
   429→
   430→| Operation                       | Conflict Rule                   |
   431→| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
   432→| Two users add different files   | Merge (union of children)       |
   433→| Two users delete same file      | Idempotent (already deleted)    |
   434→| Two users rename same file      | Last-writer-wins with timestamp |
   435→| Two users move same file        | Last-writer-wins with timestamp |
   436→| One adds, one deletes same file | Delete wins (conservative)      |
   437→
   438→### Why NOT CRDTs
   439→
   440→| Library   | Why Not for CipherBox                                                                                                                                                                                 |
   441→| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   442→| Yjs       | Designed for real-time collaborative editing (text, JSON). CipherBox doesn't need real-time -- it syncs metadata blobs via IPNS. Adding Yjs would require restructuring the entire metadata format.   |
   443→| SecSync   | Interesting E2E encrypted CRDT architecture, but beta (v0.5.0), uses XChaCha20-Poly1305 (incompatible with existing AES-256-GCM), and requires a WebSocket server. Over-engineered for metadata sync. |
   444→| Automerge | Same issues as Yjs -- designed for collaborative documents, not file metadata sync.                                                                                                                   |
   445→
   446→### Offline Queue
   447→
   448→No new library needed. Implement a simple queue using IndexedDB persistence.
   449→
   450→```typescript
   451→// Offline operation queue
   452→type QueuedOperation = {
   453→  id: string;
   454→  type: 'upload' | 'delete' | 'rename' | 'move' | 'mkdir';
   455→  payload: unknown; // operation-specific data
   456→  timestamp: number;
   457→  retryCount: number;
   458→};
   459→```
   460→
   461→Use the same `idb` library (^8.0.0) recommended for search index persistence.
   462→
   463→### Selective Sync (Desktop Only)
   464→
   465→Selective sync requires Tauri-side file system awareness. No new npm packages -- this is a Tauri/Rust concern:
   466→
   467→| Need                             | Solution                                    | Where             |
   468→| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
   469→| Sync configuration               | JSON config in app data directory           | Tauri (Rust)      |
   470→| Folder inclusion/exclusion list  | UI component + persisted config             | React + Tauri IPC |
   471→| Placeholder files (like Dropbox) | macOS: Extended attributes; Linux: symlinks | Rust FUSE layer   |
   472→
   473→### New Dependencies: NONE (beyond `idb` already counted in search)
   474→
   475→### Confidence: MEDIUM
   476→
   477→Conflict resolution design is straightforward conceptually but tricky to get right in practice, especially with encrypted metadata where you can't do server-side merging. The "merge at client-side, resign IPNS" approach needs careful testing. Flagging for deeper research during implementation.
